mechanism: A paid community sets a weekly cash prize for the best posted piece of work. The prize pool is funded from a slice of subscription revenue, members post entries, and a vote or judge picks the winner. The prize gives members a reason to post every week, which fills the feed and keeps the lower-priced rung active.
claim: A 9 dollar a month Skool community pays a weekly 750 dollar prize for posting.
why_not_testable: It needs a live community with members and a prize pool, which cannot be run keyless in a sandbox.
needs: A community platform, members and a prize budget
one_line: A weekly cash prize for the best post is the cheap mechanism that keeps a low-priced community rung busy.
idea_why: Prize rungs plausibly lift posting rates, but the break-even point depends on member count and nobody has measured it here.
breakdown: Pick a weekly theme, open a submission thread, and set a fixed prize cap that scales with a percentage of that week's subscription revenue so it can never cost more than it earns. Collect entries in the platform's own feed, then have the host or a members' vote choose a winner on a fixed day. Announce the winner publicly with the winning work so it doubles as marketing. A person is needed to judge, pay out and moderate; no script covers trust in the judging.
missing: A community with enough members for a prize to matter.

mechanism: Agent harnesses use CPU in short bursts at start-up and during tasks, and extra RAM only while a browser or computer-use task runs. The provider oversubscribes hosts by packing many sandboxes onto each machine and reclaiming memory when a task ends. Cost per sandbox is then driven by average rather than peak usage.
claim: Sandboxes for agents at under 10% of typical provider cost, averaging 0.37 dollars a month per sandbox and 0.05 to 0.10 for free-plan users.
why_not_testable: It is a hosted service needing an account, and the claim is about their fleet costs which cannot be checked from outside.
one_line: Agent sandboxes get cheap by selling average rather than peak CPU and RAM, since harnesses only spike in bursts.
idea_why: Overcommitting bursty workloads is a standard hosting trick and agent harnesses fit the pattern.
breakdown: Run many small microVMs or containers per host with memory ballooning or cgroup limits, and snapshot idle sandboxes to disk so they use no RAM. Give each a burst CPU allowance and scale RAM up only when a browser process starts. Meter real usage per sandbox to confirm the average. A hired person would handle noisy-neighbour incidents and security isolation, which no script covers.

idea_why: Letting a vision model inspect its own render and iterate is a proven way to lift front-end output.

mechanism: The language model picks which predefined behaviour-tree skill to run, and each skill checks its own execution conditions locally. When a condition fails, the skill stops immediately and returns structured failure feedback, so the model can retry or report without a round trip. A 161-task benchmark runs in text for speed and in simulation on a subset to catch perception and motion failures.
claim: A 9B model runs fully onboard a quadruped, and the design beats the best Act/ReAct baseline by about 10 and 5 points at 4B and 9B.
why_not_testable: It needs a local model and a robot or simulator, and there is no local LLM on this Mac.
needs: A local LLM and Habitat simulator
one_line: Small models act better when tools police their own preconditions and hand back structured failure reasons, not when the model rechecks everything.
idea_why: Local guards plus informative errors is a cheap, general way to make weak agents more reliable.
breakdown: Wrap each action a bot can take in a function that checks its own preconditions and returns a typed error on failure. Let the model choose only among those actions and read the typed error to decide a retry. Build a text-only task set for fast comparison and a slower real-environment set for the subset. The same pattern would suit a game bot.

mechanism: Each episode samples one hidden configuration from tens of millions of options covering layout, crafting rules, payoffs and resource dynamics, then holds it fixed over five trials. Agents must infer the rules by acting and also adapt to other agents. Eight language models are scored in homogeneous and mixed teams.
claim: Rule discovery often improves performance but does not reliably sustain cooperation, and every team exhausts the shared resource in OpenHarvest.
why_not_testable: It needs model answers from eight LLMs and a JAX environment, and there is no local LLM tonight.
needs: LLM access and the benchmark code
one_line: Language-model agents that find the hidden rules still drain the shared resource, so working out the game does not make them cooperate.
idea_why: The latent-rule sampling design is sound, but the result depends on model choice and has not been replicated.
breakdown: Define a parametrised environment generator with hidden rules, hold one sample fixed across repeated trials, and score agents on return and on shared-resource level. Run homogeneous and mixed teams of different models. Compare rule discovery against sustained cooperation. The same test shape can score any game bot that has to learn a hidden ruleset.

mechanism: The SORA token bonding curve is a smart contract with a buy price function and a sell price function, both rising roughly linearly. Reserve assets such as ETH, DAI, VAL and PSWAP are deposited to mint new XOR at the buy price and redeemed at the sell price. The gap between the two lines is the protocol's margin.
claim: A token bonding curve contract mints XOR against reserve assets and is said to boost token value.
why_not_testable: Verifying it means reading chain data for a different network and the video gives no figures to check.
one_line: SORA uses two separate buy and sell price lines on a reserve-backed curve, unlike a launchpad where one curve prices both sides.
idea_why: A reserve-backed curve with a buy-sell gap is coherent, but the value claim is not backed by any number in the clip.
breakdown: Read the contract's buy and sell price functions from the chain explorer. Record reserve balances and supply over time. Compute the spread between the two lines and the implied backing per token. A person would need to check the contract source for admin controls.

one_line: A UGC marketplace gets fast applicant volume only if it already owns a standing pool of creators.
idea_why: The model works for platforms with a creator pool, and nobody here has tested whether the volume holds for a small agency.
breakdown: Write a brief template, post it where creators already gather, and use a form to collect applications with sample reel links. Score applicants against a checklist and shortlist. Paying and contracting creators needs a person. The creator pool is the hard part and no script builds it.

mechanism: A local router handles simple commands such as opening apps or playing a playlist without any model. Harder tasks are passed to claude -p on the user's existing plan. When a task succeeds the first time, its exact steps are logged and replayed next time without the model.
claim: App launches take about 0.08 seconds, and a meeting-creation task falls from 30 seconds to 5 to 8 seconds on the second run.
why_not_testable: It needs macOS accessibility permissions and live claude -p calls on a paid plan, so it is not keyless tonight.
needs: macOS permissions and a Claude plan
one_line: A Mac assistant caches each successful task as a replayable script, so the second run skips the model and drops from 30 seconds to under 8.
idea_why: Recording a successful trace and replaying it without the model is a well known way to cut latency and cost.
breakdown: Route input through a rule-based matcher first and call the model only on a miss. When the model completes a task, store the tool-call sequence with its parameters. On a repeat, replay the sequence and fall back to the model if a step fails. Use claude -p so no API key is needed. A person would need to review stored traces for safety.
